candidates.title: Transdiagnostic factors differentially shape choices and reaction times in social evaluative learning
candidates.abstract: BackgroundLearning from feedback provided by others is important for navigating complex social environments. Aberrant processing of such social feedback is implicated in the psychopathology of several mental health disorders including social anxiety and depression. Recent psychiatric research increasingly adopts transdiagnostic approaches that examine mechanisms and constructs cutting across traditional diagnostic categories. MethodsHere, we applied reinforcement learning models together with transdiagnostic measures of psychopathology to formally assess social evaluation learning. Human participants (n = 193) completed the Social Evaluation Learning Task, learning whether computer personas ‘liked,’ ‘disliked,’ or were ‘neutral’ toward them. Participants also completed six questionnaires assessing socially relevant psychiatric traits. ResultsComputational modeling revealed that a model with separate learning parameters for positive and negative feedback best accounted for the learning behavior. Exploratory factor analysis identified three transdiagnostic factors. A factor reflecting social avoidance predicted enhanced learning from negative feedback and a reduced positive learning bias. Socially avoidant individuals with heightened negative learning rates additionally showed faster reaction times specifically in positive social contexts. A second factor linking with emotional insensitivity for others predicted a lower choice accuracy in both positively and negatively valanced conditions and was associated with faster reaction times overall. No significant associations emerged for a third factor reflecting depressive and mood-related symptoms. ConclusionsThese results demonstrate how transdiagnostic trait dimensions shape social learning mechanisms through specific behavioral and computational processes.

candidates.title: Assessing mentalization in humans and large language models
candidates.abstract: Abstract  Mentalization - the ability to infer others’ beliefs and intentions to guide one’s own choices - is a key cognitive function underlying human social interactions. Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate behaviour consistent with humans on theory-of-mind tasks, yet whether these models can guide adaptive behaviour through mentalization is unknown. Here we use two economic games with cognitive computational modeling to uncover the latent strategies underlying mentalization in LLMs. We tested individual LLM agents across four model families, DeepSeek, GPT-4.1, GPT-5 and Gemini 2.0 Flash (N = 2,099), against opponents of varying sophistication and examined whether a prompting strategy designed to elicit strategic reasoning improved performance. We benchmarked results against human participants (N = 251) as a comparative measure. Across both games, LLMs showed clear behavioural and computational signatures of mentalizing that differed markedly by model provider and size. Strategic prompting generally improved performance by inducing more sophisticated reasoning, yet the extent of the benefit differed across the two tasks. Last, GPT-5 agents flexibly adapted their recursive depth of reasoning to increasingly sophisticated opponents, demonstrating superior performance to human participants. Collectively, we demonstrate different capacities for mentalization across LLMs, and highlight cognitive computational modeling as a formal method for assessing comparative intelligence across humans and machines.

candidates.title: Do psychiatrists have a spider-sense? Clinical impressions as violations of interpersonal Bayesian expectation
candidates.abstract: Psychiatric diagnosis depends on the clinician's ability to infer mental states from complex and dynamically evolving interpersonal signals. During the psychiatric interview, clinicians do not only collect explicit symptoms; they continuously sample a rich array of non-verbal and paralinguistic cues including gaze, prosody, affective reciprocity, and interactional timing. These signals are central to psychiatric assessment, yet their contribution to diagnostic reasoning remains poorly formalized. In this Review, we propose a computational account of clinical impressions in psychiatry. We integrate evidence from phenomenological psychopathology, social cognition, and computational neuroscience. We argue that such impressions may arise when the clinician's generative model of social interaction is persistently disconfirmed by subtle deviations in interpersonal behaviour, generating high-level social prediction errors experienced as a sense of incongruity or failed attunement. We formalize this process as VIBE: Violation of Interpersonal Bayesian Expectation. VIBE denotes a pre-reflective epistemic signal generated when observed interpersonal cues deviate from the clinician's expected model of social reciprocity. It is not a diagnostic criterion but orients hypothesis generation by drawing attention to disturbances in interpersonal predictability. We hypothesize that VIBE may constitute a transdiagnostic mechanism: different disorders, from schizophrenia to autism spectrum disorder and mood disorders, may disrupt distinct dimensions of interpersonal prediction. The Praecox Feeling, first described by Rümke in 1942, can be read as the earliest clinical formalization of this process and as its schizophrenia-spectrum instance, in which the profile of interpersonal violations is consistent enough to be clinically recognizable. This framework recasts the diagnostic impression as an embodied inferential process rather than an opaque subjective faculty. Teaching clinicians to articulate, examine, and recalibrate these impressions could strengthen diagnostic reasoning, reduce bias, and improve therapeutic attunement. VIBE provides a bridge between phenomenological psychopathology and computational neuroscience, and offers a tractable, empirically testable model for studying the neurocomputational basis of psychiatric clinical judgement.

candidates.title: Beyond Average Behaviour: Trust and Reciprocity Dynamics Reveal Distinct Behavioural Phenotypes
candidates.abstract: Cooperation depends not only on how much people trust and reciprocate, but on how it is maintained and repaired after rupture. We analysed a 10-round Trust Game in participants with borderline personality disorder (BPD), an affective-symptom sample (AD), and community controls (N = 1,300 participants contributing 1,310 games; BPD n = 468, AD n = 556, controls n = 286 games), using mixed-effects and hidden Markov models. Average behaviour was broadly similar across groups, although AD trustees returned more than controls. As investors, BPD participants adjusted less to feedback than controls. Among trustees, AD differed most clearly from BPD: AD trustees followed cooperative response patterns more often, resumed cooperation more readily after exploitative returns, and had higher model-implied long-run cooperation at low and moderate partner investments. The occupancy and repair differences persisted when hidden states were estimated without diagnostic information, but not when BPD was restricted to interview-confirmed cases. AD–control differences in cooperative patterns did not persist among participants tested online. BPD–control differences in maintaining and restoring cooperation were smaller and depended on investment and hidden-state specification. Clinical differences were more evident in interaction dynamics than in average behaviour.

candidates.title: Social behavior in action video game players: the contribution of competitive personality
candidates.abstract: Abstract  Background  Research on action video game play, which encompasses first- and third-person shooter games but is not limited to those, has focused more on the cognitive than the social behavioral profile of such gamers. In parallel, research on social behavior among video game players has predominantly focused on the impact of violent video game content on aggression. The present cross-sectional study characterizes aggressive and prosocial behaviors in action video game players (AVGPs) compared with non-video game players (NVGPs) and examines whether observed group differences may be partly related to competitive personality. Methods  Adults who either frequently played action video games or seldom played video games (N = 104) completed the Competitive Reaction Time Task (CRTT), the Zurich Prosocial Game, the Money Burning Game, and the Dictator Game, together with questionnaires assessing aggressive, empathic, and competitive personality traits. Group comparisons and nested multiple regression analyses were conducted to examine the contribution of competitive personality to observed behavioral differences. Results  Compared with NVGPs, AVGPs displayed greater retaliatory behavior during the CRTT and reported higher levels of competitive personality and trait aggression. By contrast, the groups did not differ in spiteful punishment, helping behavior, altruistic sharing, or empathic personality traits. Importantly, the group differences in retaliatory behavior and trait aggression were substantially attenuated after accounting for competitive personality. Conclusions  Rather than supporting a generalized aggressive profile among AVGPs, these findings identify competitive personality as an important individual characteristic positively associated with retaliatory behavior and contributing substantially to behavioral differences that might otherwise be attributed to gaming status alone.

candidates.title: Attachment and social-interactive functioning in autistic children and adolescents: a scoping review
candidates.abstract: Background Social communication and interactive differences are core features of autism that shape developmental outcomes and quality of life. Attachment relationships may constitute important relational contexts for socio-emotional development in autistic children and adolescents.Methods A scoping review was conducted to map the literature examining associations between attachment and social-interactive functioning in autistic children and adolescents. Systematic searches of PsycINFO, Scopus, and Google Scholar identified eight eligible observational studies published since 2000. Data were extracted regarding sample characteristics, attachment measures, developmental outcomes, and key findings.Results Studies examined emotional and behavioral adjustment, emotion recognition, theory of mind, play behavior, empathy, peer relationships, and social engagement. Attachment security was generally associated with better social, emotional, and relational functioning, whereas insecure or disorganized attachment was associated with greater behavioral difficulties and reduced social reciprocity. Secure attachment was also associated with higher symbolic play, empathy, language development, and positive social interaction. However, the evidence base was limited by small samples, methodological heterogeneity, and predominantly cross-sectional designs.Conclusions Attachment may be an important relational factor in socio-emotional and social-interactive development among autistic children and adolescents. Larger longitudinal and multimethod studies are needed to clarify developmental pathways and to guide attachment-informed research and intervention.

candidates.title: Using co-created video stories to support more equitable healthcare interactions for families of autistic children with learning disabilities
candidates.abstract: Abstract  BACKGROUND Autistic children with learning disabilities have poor health outcomes and increased mortality compared to other groups, with poorer healthcare experiences. Time for Autism (TfA) is an educational intervention supporting trainee doctors to better understand and empathise with this group. Digital Story-making is a method for families of autistic children with learning disability (LD) to create positive video narratives to support more neuroaffirmative ways of engaging with professionals. OBJECTIVE We investigated the feasibility of Digital Stories to enhance the TfA intervention in supporting better understanding of the needs of this group. METHODS Three families of autistic children with LD were supported to create short Digital Stories to share with medical students visiting them in the TfA intervention. Students also created Digital Stories. Three family members and two students were interviewed to gauge the potential effects of using such stories to facilitate engagement between the groups . RESULTS Ten themes highlighted that the stories supported authentic representation of family perspectives, supported a more holistic view, powerfully supplemented written reports, presented implicit and contextual information to support better health provision, enabled parent reflection and neuroaffirmative approaches and increased reciprocity in medical interactions. Students appreciated advantages for learning and pre-visit familiarisation and suggested procedural changes for story creation by professionals. CONCLUSIONS Co-creating digital stories is a feasible way for enhancing client voice in healthcare interactions and for professional learning. They can also provide powerful guidance, both general and tailored, for adapting medical environments to better support health needs of autistic children with LD.

candidates.title: Development and validation of a task for assessing help-seeker relational dynamics
candidates.abstract: Self-other evaluations play a crucial role in understanding psychiatric disorders and improving collaboration between service users and providers. However, experimental paradigms of such relational processes tend to have low reliability and ecological validity. Quantitative analyses can validate the task’s measurement properties while qualitative analyses can empower service users to provide novel insights about task development and interpretation. In this study, we use both quantitative and qualitative analyses to develop the “Helping Task” based on the iterated prisoner’s dilemma. In this task, help-seeking participants knowingly engaged in an asymmetric relationship with a computerized help-provider, in which both parties invested effort (points). Initial qualitative feedback from 17 individuals (15 ‘neurotypical’, 2 having lived experience of relational difficulties) was used to refine key task properties (like task instructions, interface labels, and general navigation). Subsequent thematic analyses revealed that these participants interpreted helping exchanges through expectations about reciprocity, moral obligations, and underlying mental intentions, mirroring descriptions of real helping relationships. Moreover, quantitative analyses of 30 online participants validated the task’s sensitivity to helper behaviour and the within-session reliability of mean trust, decision satisfaction, and intended effort. Finally, computational analyses revealed probabilistic states in which trust, decision satisfaction, and effort were jointly lower or higher, indicating that self-other evaluations were linked to willingness to invest in the relationship. These findings support the reliability and validity of the Helping Task and pave the way for computational studies of self-other evaluations in helping relationships.

candidates.title: Meeting LLMs for the First Time: Understanding Trust Formation and Adjustment Among Older Adults in China
candidates.abstract: Against the backdrop of rapid population aging and the proliferation of Large Language Models (LLMs) in China, this study investigates the dynamics of trust formation and adjustment among Chinese older adults during their initial encounters with LLM agents. Through in-depth interviews conducted before, during, and immediately after 30 older adults’ first interactions with six widely used Chinese LLM applications, followed by second interviews with 26 participants, the study examines how trust was initially formed and adjusted over the short term. Findings reveal that pre-interaction responses were predominantly characterized by low interest and skepticism, rooted in sociocultural perceptions rather than just technological barriers. Analysis identified four technological factors associated with participants’ trust-related judgments during engagement, including personalization, anthropomorphism, conversationality, and response latency. Longitudinal analysis identified three behavioral patterns of trust adjustment: Limited Correction, Collaborative Reciprocity, and Cognitive Entrenchment. These findings advance theoretical understanding of trust adjustment and calibration-related processes and offer design implications for building more trustworthy LLMs.

candidates.title: SYSTEMIC CENTRODYNAMIC MECHANICS (SCM)
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.abstract: Systemic Centrodynamic Mechanics (SCM) is proposed as a systems-theoretic framework for examining how internal states, behavioral outputs, interpersonal interactions, feedback processes, contextual constraints, and social structures jointly shape the dynamics of human relationships. Its central research problem is whether a compact functional construct, provisionally called the Primary Systemic Actuator (PSA), can explain behavioral initiation, persistence, regulation, and withdrawal beyond what is explained by established constructs and competing models.SCM begins from the observation that dyadic interactions may generate feedback: the behavior of one individual can alter the subsequent state and behavior of another, whose response can in turn affect the first individual. Such interactions may be reinforcing, balancing, delayed, asymmetric, nonlinear, or unstable. The framework also retains subjective and sociological variables, including love, altruistic motivation, self-interest, sacrifice, satisfaction, trust, expectations, perceived duty, social norms, and concern for another person's welfare. These variables are treated as distinct constructs requiring operational definitions and empirical measurement, not as interchangeable forms of physical energy.The manuscript develops a seven-layer research architecture spanning system boundaries, measurement, individual behavioral regulation, dyadic dynamics, nonlinear transitions, network-level emergence, and empirical validation. It specifies candidate state-space equations, feedback models, stability conditions, decision models, and network extensions. These formulations are hypotheses and analytical tools, not evidence that a universal return mechanism exists. Conservation of energy is not used to infer psychological reciprocity, and the existence of feedback is not assumed to imply positive-sum outcomes.The proposed framework is scientifically assessable only if its constructs are identifiable, its parameters estimable, its predictions distinguishable from those of competing explanations, and its claims open to falsification. No empirical dataset is analyzed in this conceptual manuscript; therefore, all substantive mechanisms remain provisional pending operationalization, preregistered tests, and replication.Keywords: Systemic Centrodynamic Mechanics; systems theory; cybernetics; feedback; dynamical systems; social exchange; altruism; self-interest; behavioral regulation; social networks; stability; falsifiability.

candidates.title: Practical Identifiability of a Minimal Adaptive Learning-Gain Model for Binary Feedback: A Simulation Study
candidates.abstract: Social learning is jointly determined by several computationally distinct quantities—baseline belief (prior mean), sensitivity to feedback (learning gain), and the temporal uncertainty of belief (drift)—which are rarely separated in empirical designs. Here we systematically characterise the practical identifiability and predictive adequacy of a minimal four-parameter adaptive learning-gain model of binary feedback: a latent belief v_t about the probability of a positive outcome is carried forward deterministically between observations while an internal confidence-precision state decays by a per-trial amount ω, and the belief is updated by a learning gain λ from a deterministic prior mean μ with initial confidence precision σ; σ, ω and λ are model-defined internal quantities, not validated psychological constructs. The simulated process is self-reinforcing: the same latent state both generates the binary outcome and represents the learner’s belief, so the model does not represent inference about an independently evolving social environment. The study is therefore an analysis of a phenomenological adaptive filter under a specified binary stochastic process: its update equations are deliberately chosen rather than derived from the Bernoulli–logistic likelihood, and it does not reduce to a standard hierarchical Gaussian filter. Using fixed-seed simulation studies, we report four findings. First, joint maximum-likelihood recovery is poor. On the 24-condition parameter grid at T=80 (100 independent replications per condition), the belief mean μ shows comparatively smaller errors but is still not reliably recovered; σ and ω show near-zero tolerance-based recovery that stays at most 0.002 across tolerance thresholds of 0.3, 0.6 and 1.0 transformed units, whereas λ recovery is low but not near-zero and increases with tolerance (0.078, 0.182 and 0.263 at tolerances 0.3, 0.6 and 1.0). Boundary convergence is strongest for σ (upper bound) and ω (lower bound), whereas λ boundary solutions are not uniform across grid conditions. In a separate single-parameter-vector experiment that varies trial length (T∈{40,80,120,240,480}), extending the sequence alone does not repair recovery of the positive parameters, including λ. Tolerance recovery concerns point estimates only; calibrated interval coverage is not evaluated and is not substituted by a flat profile or a boundary estimate. Second, profile-likelihood and trade-off diagnostics show flat likelihood regions for σ and ω, with an asymmetric profile for λ that constrains its upper range but is uninformative over its low range; the flat σ–ω geometry replicates in a second, low-gain regime (a within-study replication, not a claim across the full condition grid), whereas the exact steepness of the λ profile is regime-dependent. Three optimisers converge to the same boundary solution, and the fitted estimates cannot reliably rank individual simulated subjects either. These patterns support weak practical identifiability under the tested design, not structural non-identifiability; no formal structural identifiability analysis is performed, so a structural claim is not made. Third, a fitting-parity audit found and corrected a return-order defect in the fixed-gain candidate: its fitted parameters were returned with σ and ω interchanged, which artificially raised that candidate’s fitted block loss. Under the corrected fit, overall block discrimination is 67/150 = 0.45 under the original wider bounds and 72/150 = 0.48 under common fitting bounds matched to the proposed model (56 common forecast observations per dataset, each scored exactly once, with an automated index check confirming no fit–forecast overlap and no look-ahead), modestly above the 0.33 chance level; a calibrated permutation test that preserves the asymmetric winner marginals is significant (p = 0.0011 and p < 0.001). This above-chance accuracy is almost entirely attributable to Rescorla–Wagner (0.88–0.90 correct), whereas the adaptive filter and its nested fixed-gain restriction remain heavily confused (row-wise accuracies 0.18–0.22 and 0.24–0.36, neither significant), and the result is robust to the fitting bounds (row-wise p-values are descriptive and uncorrected; none of this establishes model equivalence). Fourth, across 50 independent held-out datasets the model shows no predictive advantage over a training-set empirical-frequency baseline (the paired 95% confidence interval spans zero under both normal-approximation and bootstrap estimation; the proportion of datasets won is not used as evidence of superiority), and a paired ablation shows no consistent predictive gain from the added update components and no improvement in parameter stability; no predictive advantage over this empirical-frequency baseline has therefore been demonstrated.

candidates.title: GPT-4 reasons like infants about objects but not agents
candidates.abstract: Theory of Mind (ToM) is central to human social cognition and is critical for successfully navigating the social world. However, most work to date has explored explicit ToM in AI, particularly with large language models (LLMs), and has found mixed results. In contrast, decades of developmental psychology research with human infants has found remarkable, early-emerging implicit ToM. However, little work has explored implicit ToM in LLMs. The current study investigates implicit social reasoning abilities in GPT-4 using model-facing versions of classic infant experiments. In Experiment 1, we explored GPT-4’s implicit ToM abilities across four social reasoning tasks adapted from infant paradigms. In Experiment 2, we explored whether GPT-4 was capable of physical reasoning to contrast with social reasoning in Experiments 1 and 2. Across these three experiments, our results suggest that there may be domain differences in GPT-4’s reasoning abilities, such that GPT-4 struggled with social reasoning tasks despite performing very well on physical reasoning tasks. These findings highlight the importance of systematic exploration of social reasoning in LLMs and provide insight into potential deficits in GPT-4’s social reasoning abilities.

candidates.title: In-group affiliation enhances vicarious fear learning in children
candidates.abstract: This study examined the role of in-group and out-group membership in vicarious fear learning in children. Ninety-two children (46 boys, 46 girls, aged 6-10 years) observed fearful reactions to novel animals (a quokka and a cuscus) from either in-group or out-group models. The in-group and out-group identification were manipulated using McGuire et al.'s (2015) drawing competition task. Fear beliefs and avoidance preferences were measured before and after vicarious learning. Results indicated a significant increase in fear beliefs and avoidance preferences for the fear-paired animal compared to the unpaired animal following in-group modelling, but not following out-group modelling. These findings suggest that in-group affiliation enhances the effects of vicarious fear learning, highlighting the role of social group dynamics in emotional and behavioural responses to fear. Additionally, behavioural inhibition was found to be negatively correlated with fear beliefs and avoidance preferences in the in-group condition, suggesting that participants with higher behavioural inhibition were less fearful of the fear-paired animals, and showed less avoidance of the fear-paired animal. The study contributes to our understanding of how social identity can shape fear acquisition in children.

candidates.title: Replicator--Mutator Dynamics on Networks with Spatial Nonlocality: Theory and Applications
candidates.abstract: Abstract  The replicator--mutator model provides a general framework for studying the emergence of social norms and dominant behavioral patterns in networked populations. In the traditional network formulation, mutation and observational learning operate through nearest-neighbor interactions. In realistic settings, however, agents may also be influenced by others beyond their immediate neighbors, with the strength of influence typically decaying with distance. Here we investigate how evolutionary dynamics change when these nonlocal interactions are incorporated explicitly. We introduce a generalized interaction operator based on $d$-path Laplacians, which combines interactions across all shortest-path distances. We then analyze how the range of the coupling affects evolutionary behavior on different network topologies. Our analytical results relate mutation-induced mixing and local convergence to the spectral structure of the corresponding nonlocal random-walk Laplacian. Numerical experiments show that stronger nonlocality reduces the mutation intensity required to attain high diversity and may produce an abrupt transition from behavioral flocking to an almost uniform distribution of behaviors. Thus, long-range influence promotes globalization in the sense of increased effective diversity together with greater homogeneity of behavioral frequencies.

candidates.title: Insights on Designing the MINT (Micro-Interventions for Navigating Tension) Chatbot System for Stress Management: Collaborative Autoethnography
candidates.abstract: BackgroundDigital microinterventions are increasingly used to support stress self-management in everyday life. While previous research has examined their feasibility, adherence, and preliminary effectiveness, much less is known about how these interventions are experienced over extended periods of real-world use.ObjectiveThis study used collaborative autoethnography (CAE) to examine the everyday experience of living with MINT (Micro-Interventions for Navigating Tension), a Telegram-based chatbot for stress management. Our goal was not to evaluate clinical outcomes but to understand how scheduled microinterventions fit into everyday life, when they were ignored, and when people relied on other ways of coping instead, and to identify implications for the design of future digital mental health tools.MethodsWe conducted a 4-week CAE involving 5 digital mental health researchers, who used the MINT chatbot as both participants and researchers. The experience was documented through multiple qualitative and quantitative sources, including reflective diaries, ecological momentary assessments (EMAs), workshop discussions, and wearable data, and analyzed collaboratively using reflexive thematic analysis (RTA).ResultsSix interconnected themes described how MINT was experienced in everyday life: (T1) the importance of timing and emotional receptivity, (T2) the need for reciprocity and relational continuity, (T3) the tendency to favor existing coping strategies over suggested exercises, (T4) the meaning of nonengagement during periods of high stress, (T5) the collapse of self-initiated use after reminders were removed, and (T6) how everyday experiences with consumer wearables and general-purpose large language models reshaped expectations of digital mental health systems.ConclusionsOur findings show that CAE complements conventional evaluations of digital mental health interventions by revealing aspects of everyday use that are difficult to capture through feasibility studies, large-scale trials, or looking at usage data. Beyond the specific case of MINT, they suggest that future stress-management systems should better account for users' receptivity, provide greater continuity across interactions, build on existing coping strategies, and help users move from externally prompted engagement to autonomous self-management.

candidates.title: Implementing Pay-it-Forward STI Testing: A Mixed-Methods Evaluation in Community-Based Organizations and STI Clinics in China
candidates.abstract: Abstract  Background  Pay-it-forward is an implementation strategy that offers individuals a health service as a gift and then invites voluntary contributions to support subsequent users. Although prior trials have demonstrated its effectiveness in increasing sexually transmitted infection (STI) testing, little is known about pay-it-forward implementation in diverse settings. Methods  We conducted a convergent mixed-methods evaluation guided by the RE-AIM framework. Data was collected from the PIONEER trial, which evaluated a pay-it-forward strategy to promote STI testing in two settings in China: community-based organizations (CBOs) and STI clinics. Quantitative data from 800 trial participants (400 CBOs, 400 clinics) assessed reach, uptake, donation behavior, and participant understanding. Implementers (n = 34) were surveyed to assess organizational readiness. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with implementers (n = 10) to explore adoption processes, workflow adaptations, and perceptions of sustainability, as well as with trial participants (n = 24) to understand their experiences with pay-it-forward. Results  Test uptake in pay-it-forward arm was high in both settings (CBO: 90.8%; clinic: 97%), though each setting reached distinct populations. CBOs primarily engaged men who have sex with men and first-time testers, while clinics reached more men with multiple concurrent sex partners. Barriers and facilitators to adoption differed by setting. CBOs had strong mission alignment but chronic staffing shortages, while clinics required leadership approval, multi-department coordination, and implementer motivation to sustain delivery. Clinics frequently abbreviated procedures, including providing full explanations of pay-it-forward, due to workflow pressures. Fewer than half of participants (41%) fully understood the pay-it-forward strategy in both settings. Donation rates were modest and did not differ significantly between settings (CBO: 16.8%; clinic: 21.8%; p = 0.088), though CBO donors contributed larger amounts on average (0.8 vs. 0.4 USD); together, donations covered the cost of approximately 22 additional tests. Qualitative data suggested CBO donations were motivated by gratitude and a sense of community reciprocity, while clinic donations, though somewhat more frequent, were tempered by implementer caution around patient trust and fears of appearing to solicit money. Conclusions  Pay-it-forward can increase STI testing in both community and clinic settings; however, test receipt through pay-it-forward does not ensure participants will understand the participatory implementation strategy. CBOs can leverage preexisting connections and trust with marginalized communities to implement pay-it-forward, but resource limitations remain a substantial barrier. The large patient volumes in STI clinics pose a challenge to consistent and faithful implementation of pay-it-forward. Effective scale-up will require setting-specific strategies that address staffing constraints in CBOs and leadership and workflow barriers in STI clinics. Our findings may be relevant to implementation scientists working across clinic and community settings.

candidates.title: Gamified spatial‑participatory model for urban social cohesion in a post‑conflict city: Bridging accessibility, inclusion, and intergroup trust through co‑design in Kabul
candidates.abstract: Post‑conflict cities exhibit profound socio‑spatial fractures, institutional weakness, and eroded public trust. Conventional planning repeatedly fails to address ethnic segregation, accessibility disparities, and social fragmentation. The aim of this study is to propose and empirically validate an integrated model, the Gamified Spatial-Participatory Model (GSPM), that combines spatial justice theory, participatory co-design, and conflict-sensitive gamification to foster social cohesion. Using Kabul, Afghanistan, as a paradigmatic case, a sequential mixed‑methods design was employed. Quantitative spatial diagnostics mapped severe accessibility deficits, while qualitative inquiry identified deep trust deficits and cultural barriers; these jointly informed gamified co‑design workshops as the intervention. Pilot results provide strong preliminary evidence of GSPM efficacy: 90% of participants reported substantially increased engagement; gamification correlated strongly with intergroup trust (r = 0.76, p < 0.01); perceived accessibility improved by 38% in intervention areas. Critically, 70% of women and 55% of ethnic minorities reported meaningfully stronger belonging. The study demonstrates that this approach shifts planning epistemology from technocratic to deeply human, operationalising spatial justice in fragile settings, and offers transferable principles for fostering inclusion in divided urban contexts.

candidates.title: Traditional Games in Physical Education: Motor Skills, Fitness, Social Learning, and Cultural Sustainability
candidates.venue: International Journal of Humanities Education and Social Sciences
candidates.abstract: Traditional games offer culturally meaningful movement experiences for physical education (PE), yet their use in school lessons remains inconsistent and their outcomes are assessed unevenly. This review synthesised recent evidence on traditional games in relation to fundamental movement skills, physical fitness, participation, social learning, and cultural sustainability. A structured narrative review examined 24 peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2020 and 2026 and one World Health Organization guideline. Searches conducted in October 2026 used English and Indonesian terms across journal publisher portals, DOI-linked records, PubMed, and scholarly web indexing. Evidence was organised thematically without calculating a pooled effect estimate. The reviewed studies generally associated traditional games with opportunities to practise hopping, running, balance, coordination, agility, and object control. Several school-based studies also reported increased participation, motivation, cooperation, and positive peer interaction. Games such as engklek, gobak sodor, bentengan, and bakiak connected movement practice with teamwork, decision-making, and local cultural knowledge. However, small samples, short intervention durations, single-group pretest–posttest designs, and inconsistent outcome measures limited conclusions about causal and long-term effects. The evidence supports the pedagogical potential of traditional games while indicating the need for more rigorous evaluation. Their integration into PE should involve purposeful learning tasks with explicit movement objectives, safe and inclusive rule modifications, observable assessment criteria, and reflection on cultural meaning. Future research should employ controlled and longitudinal designs, consistent motor-skill measures, and broader regional representation to strengthen the evidence base.

candidates.title: Are You Ready for Autonomous Driving? The Role of Experiential Learning in Enhancing Trust and Understandability
candidates.abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have transformed transportation, yet human drivers remain essential. In level 3 autonomous vehicles, drivers must respond to takeover requests and share driving responsibilities, but effective strategies for training them remain poorly understood. This study examines how learning style (experiential vs. observational) and message framing (gain vs. loss) influence drivers' learning experience and performance in autonomous driving. In a 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment with 121 participants, experiential learning was more effective than observational learning in enhancing drivers' social presence, trust, and understanding of their roles. Loss-framed messages led to higher cognitive load, greater risk perception, and faster reaction times than gain-framed messages. Learning style and message framing interacted to affect trust, and trust mediated the effect of learning style on understandability. These findings integrate learning theory with message framing and offer practical guidance for designing safety training programs for autonomous driving.

candidates.title: The Role of the Family in Bullying Prevention in Early Childhood
candidates.abstract: Bullying in early childhood is a real phenomenon with long-term psychosocial consequences that is frequently overlooked. This literature review analyzes the family’s role in preventing early childhood bullying through three focal areas: the role of parenting styles in children’s aggressive tendencies, family environment factors as primary bullying predictors, and parental attachment’s role in empathy development. Twenty-three sources were selected based on topic relevance and full-text availability, covering publications from 2011–2025 across multiple countries including Indonesia, Norway, China, and Spain. The review employs Bronfenbrenner’s Ecological Systems Theory, Bandura’s Social Learning Theory, and Bowlby’s Attachment Theory, yielding a four-pillar conceptual model: authoritative parenting, elimination of environmental risk factors, attachment reinforcement through emotion coaching, and instillation of religious-moral values as the macrosystem foundation.

candidates.title: A játékos kihívások szerepe az elmélyült kémiatanulásban. Egy empirikus kutatás eredményei: The Role of Game-Based Challenges in Deep Chemistry Learning. Findings from an Empirical Study
candidates.abstract: The effectiveness of chemistry learning can be significantly influenced not only by the content of the curriculum but also by the learning environment and the design of tasks. In our research, we examined the student experiences resulting from various types of chemistry challenges embedded in a game-based framework. The study involved ninth-grade students from a secondary school in Eger. We used questionnaire-based data collection and focus group discussions to explore students' experiences. Based on the results, the variety of tasks, the appropriate difficulty level of the challenges, and the game-like framework all contributed to the students' active participation. According to the students’ reports, sustained attention was present during the completion of the tasks. Social cooperation also emerged as an important element; at the same time, student feedback highlighted that the deliberate planning of cooperative tasks is essential. The research contributes to the design of gamified chemistry learning environments, with particular attention to the variety of task types, differentiated difficulty, and opportunities for social learning. KIVONATA kémiatanulás eredményességét nemcsak a tananyag tartalma, hanem a tanulási környezet és a feladatok kialakítása is jelentősen befolyásolhatja. Kutatásunkban azt vizsgáltuk, hogy a különböző jellegű, játékos keretbe ágyazott kémiai kihívások milyen tanulói tapasztalatokat eredményeznek. A vizsgálatban egy egri középiskola kilencedik évfolyamos tanulói vettek részt. A tanulói élmények feltárására kérdőíves adatfelvételt és fókuszcsoportos beszélgetést alkalmaztunk. Az eredmények alapján a feladatok változatossága, a kihívások megfelelő nehézségi szintje, valamint a játékos keret egyaránt hozzájárult a tanulók aktív részvételéhez. A diákok beszámolói alapján a feladatok megoldása során jelen volt a tartós figyelem. A társas együttműködés szintén fontos elemként jelent meg, ugyanakkor a tanulói visszajelzések rámutattak arra, hogy a kooperatív feladatok tudatos tervezése nélkülözhetetlen. A kutatás hozzájárul a játékosított kémiatanulási környezetek tervezéséhez, különös tekintettel a feladattípusok változatosságára, a differenciált nehézségre és a társas tanulás lehetőségeire.

candidates.title: THE ATTACHMENT-SIGNAL BREACH REINFORCEMENT PRINCIPLE (ASBRP)
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.abstract: This paper proposes the Attachment-Signal Breach Reinforcement Principle (ASBRP), a conditional theoretical framework developed from the primary case study entitled THE BROKEN-PROMISE PARADOX (BPP). The primary case concerns a person who returns before the end of a declared period of reduced contact and explains the return through intense attachment, longing, or emotional dissatisfaction in the other person's absence. The central proposed mechanism is that an act interpreted as a commitment breach may simultaneously function as an attachment-related signal. Consequently, perceived relational acceptance, benevolence, or closeness may increase even while perceived commitment reliability decreases. Two connected mechanisms are distinguished. The first, Breach-to-Attachment Signal Conversion, specifies the proposed transformation from commitment deviation to an interpreted attachment signal. The second, Breach-Associated System Reinforcement, specifies the additional conditions under which changed relational engagement may affect coordination or another independently defined system-level outcome. The second mechanism is not inferred automatically from the first.The paper operationalizes the principal constructs, defines a conditional signal-activation index, specifies candidate state-transition equations, states falsifiable hypotheses, and identifies semantic, causal, temporal, and mathematical boundary conditions. It also proposes a research design and a reproducible computational template. The equations are candidate formalizations rather than empirically estimated laws. No original empirical dataset, validated parameter estimates, or causal findings are claimed. Existing research on prosocial deception, benevolence-integrity conflicts, and trust repair provides relevant comparisons and limits the scope of any originality claim. ASBRP is therefore presented as a testable, case-anchored theoretical proposal rather than an established universal law.

candidates.title: 神经递质与内分泌的动力系统:多巴胺奖励预测误差、血清素稳态、HPA轴异态负荷与睾酮挑战假说的数学建模及东方调心观 | Dynamical Systems of Neurotransmitters and Endocrinology: Dopamine Reward Prediction Error, Serotonergic Homeostasis, HPA-Axis Allostatic Load and the Challenge Hypothesis, Read Beside East Asian Classics of Mind Regulation
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.abstract: Popular accounts often treat dopamine, cortisol, testosterone and serotonin as switches to be turned up or down. This book puts them back into their feedback loops and examines them with dynamical-systems, reinforcement-learning and optimisation models: the reward prediction error and temporal-difference learning of Schultz, Dayan and Montague, and how the average-reward model of Niv and colleagues explains the negative error of ordinary effort after frequent intense stimulation, read beside Solomon and Corbit's opponent-process theory; a model of the CRH–ACTH–cortisol feedback loop with glucocorticoid-receptor down-regulation (bistability and a tipping point in stress frequency), how allostatic load is scored, and the meta-analytic evidence that chronic stress in humans can show up as either raised or lowered cortisol; Wingfield's challenge hypothesis, the measured size of testosterone effects (Eisenegger's ultimatum game, the winner–loser effect, the failed replication of power posing and the marginal support for the dual-hormone hypothesis), HPA inhibition of the HPG axis, and challenge versus threat appraisal; tryptophan-depletion studies, the umbrella review of serotonin and depression, and a light-phase model of ipRGCs and the circadian clock; the resonance of the baroreflex loop at about six breaths a minute and what it implies for measurement; and the absence of a single optimal state in the sense of a Pareto front. The eight chapters are read beside Mencius on nourishing the flood-like qi, the Suwen on tranquil emptiness and the Zhuangzi's wooden cockerel, with the limits of the analogies, and end with a four-step check of personal daily rhythm (morning light, blocking high-frequency fragments, slow breathing and recovery, complete and regular sleep) and a pre-registered randomised controlled trial comparing morning daylight plus 0.1 Hz slow breathing with usual routine in high-stress founders, with resting heart-rate variability (lnRMSSD) as primary outcome and the cortisol awakening response as secondary outcome (decision rule written as code). Marked boxes separate published evidence, runnable Python calculations (14 programs, all checked), classical sources and the author's hypotheses. Health notice: this book is not medical advice, makes no diagnosis, gives no doses of any drug, hormone or supplement, and does not claim that any practice treats any disease. 流行说法常把多巴胺、皮质醇、睾酮和血清素当作可以分别调高调低的开关。本书把它们放回所在的反馈回路,用动力系统、强化学习与优化模型考察:舒尔茨、达扬与蒙塔古的奖励预测误差与时间差分学习,以及尼夫等人的平均奖励率模型如何解释高频强刺激之后日常努力的负向误差,并与所罗门和科比特的对手过程理论并读;CRH–ACTH–皮质醇负反馈回路与糖皮质激素受体下调的模型(双稳态与压力频率的转折点)、异态负荷指数的计算方法,以及慢性压力在人类中既可表现为皮质醇升高也可表现为降低的元分析证据;温菲尔德的挑战假说、睾酮效应量的实证大小(艾森内格的最后通牒博弈、胜负效应与力量姿势的重复失败、双激素假说的边缘支持)、HPA 对 HPG 轴的交叉抑制与挑战—威胁评估;色氨酸耗竭研究、血清素与抑郁关系的伞形综述、ipRGC 与昼夜时钟的光相位模型;压力反射回路在每分钟约 6 次呼吸时的共振及其对测量指标的含义;以及帕累托前沿意义上不存在单一最优状态。 八章与《孟子·公孙丑上》养浩然之气、《素问·上古天真论》恬惔虚无和《庄子·达生》木鸡并读,并说明类比的限度;最后给出个人日常节律四步核查(晨间光照、阻断高频碎片刺激、慢呼吸与恢复、睡眠完整与规律),以及一项比较晨间自然光加 0.1 赫兹慢呼吸与常规作息对高压创业者静息心率变异性(lnRMSSD,主要结局)与晨起皮质醇反应(次要结局)影响的预注册随机对照试验方案(判定规则写成代码)。书中以标注框区分已发表的证据、可运行的 Python 计算(14 段程序,全部核对)、原典与作者的假说。健康提示:本书不是医疗建议,不作诊断,不给任何药物、激素或补充剂剂量,不声称任何练习能治疗任何疾病。 Disclosure. The author uses this book as the methodological basis of his community cognition courses, 5D Ascension Cards (Dimensional Shift Card Decks) and the Yafu AI knowledge base, and so has a direct commercial interest in its subject and in the result of the Chapter 8 trial. The book promotes no course, card deck or product and makes no health or therapeutic claim; the trial is designed to be run and analysed by researchers independent of the author's business; all the code and the study protocol are published openly for anyone to check. Note on writing. The text, boxes and code were drafted with an AI writing tool from the author's title, framework and notes; the author is responsible for reviewing and revising them and for checking every source. candidates.title: Hierarchical Interoceptive–Social Inference Dysregulation: A Computational Psychiatry Framework for Borderline Personality Disorder with Level-1 Active Inference Simulation and Implications for Cluster B Pathology
candidates.abstract: Abstract Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD), the prototypic Cluster B condition, is characterised by profound instability in affect, self-image, and interpersonal relationships, including rapid oscillation between idealisation and devaluation. Despite decades of neurobiological and psychotherapeutic research, no unified mechanistic theory accounts for the simultaneous presence of interoceptive dysregulation, interpersonal hypersensitivity, unstable identity, and splitting. Here we (i) review the hot research topics in Cluster B personality disorders in the recent literature, including triple-network neuroimaging dysconnectivity, allostatic interoceptive overload, and computational psychiatry approaches; (ii) identify the critical gap — the absence of a formal mechanistic account coupling interoceptive and social predictive hierarchies; (iii) propose the Hierarchical Interoceptive–Social Inference Dysregulation (HISID) framework, positing that BPD arises from a precision dissociation in which interoceptive precision is chronically suppressed while social-threat precision is pathologically elevated, leaving the self-model anchored exclusively to volatile social-affective inputs; and (iv) present a Level-1 computational simulation implementing two active inference agents — a healthy control (HC) and a BPD agent characterised by suppressed interoceptive precision, asymmetric social-threat amplification, a bimodal (splitting) social prior, and a hysteresis commitment mechanism — embedded in a 300-trial social-threat paradigm. While the HISID framework is introduced within the broader context of Cluster B personality disorders, the formal theory, parameterisation, simulations, and empirical predictions presented in this paper are specific to BPD as the prototypic Cluster B condition. Extension of the precision-dissociation formalism to narcissistic, antisocial, and histrionic personality disorders — each of which is predicted to occupy a distinct parametric region within the same generative architecture — is deferred to subsequent work. Across $$n=40$$ agents per group, the BPD agent produces a 4.22 $$\times $$ increase in self-model variance, a 10.33 $$\times $$ increase in per-agent median threat-recovery time, and a 4.45 $$\times $$ increase in unweighted cumulative prediction-error accumulation (alongside a 2.61 $$\times $$ increase in precision-weighted free energy; the unweighted measure is reported as a control on precision-induced mechanical scaling). A factorial control study crossing precision profile with generative architecture decomposes the BPD phenotype into distinct contributions: identity-instability variance is driven primarily by the bimodal-prior architecture, whereas threat-recovery slowing is driven primarily by the asymmetric threat-conditional precision, with a super-additive interaction in the full agent. These differences are large and internally consistent within the simulation and constitute demonstrations of model sufficiency, not empirical theory validation. A sensitivity analysis across a $$3\times 3$$ precision grid confirms qualitative robustness. A key architectural finding is that the bimodal prior requires Bayesian mixture belief updating with hysteresis commitment — not gradient descent — providing a candidate formalisation of splitting as discrete pole-occupancy inference. The HISID framework, grounded in the Free Energy Principle, generates five operationalised empirical predictions testable with existing neuroimaging and computational phenotyping methods.

candidates.title: Who Knows What - and What Does It Support? Perspective-Bounded Evidence Calibration for Multimodal Theory of Mind
candidates.abstract: Theory of Mind (ToM), the ability to infer others' beliefs, goals, and intentions, is a cornerstone of social intelligence. Multimodal ToM requires inferring an agent's mental state from evidence that is available to that agent, rather than from the complete episode observed by the solver. Existing LLM-based and Bayesian model-based approaches reconstruct global event traces, yet they do not explicitly distinguish objective events from agent-admissible evidence during hypothesis evaluation. Consequently, agent-inaccessible events or semantically misaligned actions and utterances may influence the inferred belief, goal, or social intention, leading to perspective leakage and source or route confusion. We formulate this limitation as an evidence-admissibility problem: evidence should contribute to a mental-state hypothesis only when it is accessible to the relevant agent, preserves its information source, and is diagnostic of the queried mental-state variable. To operationalize this principle, we propose PIP-ToM, an evidence-admissibility interface that constructs agent-specific evidence stores, aligns them with structured mental-state claims, and calibrates model-based hypothesis scores while preserving the underlying Bayesian inference process. PIP-ToM with GPT-4o outperforms existing ToM methods across MuMA-ToM, MMToM-QA, and Hi-ToM, achieving average accuracies of 92.56%, 95.00%, and 95.00%, respectively.

candidates.title: Generative AI Factors, Cognitive Engagement, and Patient Safety Learning in Medical Education: Mixed Methods Study
candidates.abstract: BackgroundGenerative AI (GenAI) is increasingly used during medical training, including clerkships in which learning takes place alongside supervised patient care. Its educational value may depend on how students interpret, verify, and regulate AI-generated output.ObjectiveThis study explored medical clerkship students' accounts of GenAI use and examined how GenAI-related factors were associated with self-reported ward-based infection-prevention practice through self-efficacy in AI-generated usage and perceived AI self-control balance.MethodsWe used an exploratory sequential mixed methods design. Eight medical clerkship students with experience using GenAI participated in semistructured interviews analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. The qualitative findings were considered alongside theory and prior evidence to specify a theory-based model. This model was subsequently examined through an online cross-sectional survey of 214 eligible students recruited from 5 private universities in the Jakarta Metropolitan Area, Indonesia. Quantitative associations were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling with bootstrapping.ResultsThe interviews yielded 16 themes concerning appraisal of AI-generated output, confidence in using GenAI, interaction control, patient-safety awareness, and infection-prevention learning. The structural paths were unchanged, although 3 low-loading measurement indicators were removed before hypothesis testing. Global model fit was limited (estimated-model standardized root mean square residual 0.089; normed fit index 0.691), and pairwise residual fit was not used as a retention criterion. Explainability quality exposure and perceived algorithmic fairness were positively associated with both self-efficacy and perceived AI self-control balance. Trust calibration literacy was associated with self-efficacy but not perceived AI self-control balance. Privacy concern was positively associated with self-efficacy (β=0.294, PConclusionsSelf-efficacy was the more consistent pathway linking students' appraisals of GenAI with self-reported ward-based infection-prevention practice. By integrating students' accounts with quantitative testing of a theory-based model, this study extends research that has largely focused on GenAI acceptance and general educational use by examining a safety-oriented outcome within clinical training. The findings add evidence on the human factors through which GenAI use may relate to patient-safety learning, although the cross-sectional, self-reported data do not establish causal or clinical effects. Medical schools and teaching hospitals could use these findings to inform clerkship guidance on supervised verification of AI-generated output, patient-data protection, alignment with local protocols, and continued human responsibility for clinical decisions.

candidates.title: Reputation-Aware Distributed Filtering for Nonlinear Bias-Corrupted Systems Over Sensor Networks Under Event-Triggered Mechanism
candidates.abstract: This article is concerned with the reputation-aware Kalman-type distributed filtering (RAKTDF) problem for a class of nonlinear bias-corrupted systems (NBCSs) with a dynamical event-triggered mechanism (DETM). First, a representative unknown input, namely the dynamical bias, is introduced, which is evolved by a dynamical equation with Gaussian white noise. A DETM is employed to regulate the frequency of data transmission so that data conflict and network congestion are avoided. In order to identify and eliminate abnormal data from neighbors, a trust-based scoring strategy, referred to as the reputation-aware mechanism, is modeled and utilized to improve the accuracy of the filtering algorithm. The RAKTDF algorithm is recursively developed such that the covariance upper bound of the filtering error dynamic (CUBFED) is derived, after which the filter gain is determined by minimizing the trace of the CUBFED. Furthermore, a sufficient condition is established to guarantee the boundedness of the filtering error dynamics. Finally, an illustrative example is provided to verify the effectiveness of the proposed RAKTDF algorithm.

candidates.title: The Evolution of Financial Time Series Forecasting: From Classical Econometrics to Temporal Foundation Models and Multimodal LLMs
candidates.abstract: Financial time series forecasting sits at the intersection of applied mathematics, econometrics, and machine learning. The data generating processes involved are characterized by non-stationarity, regime-dependent volatility clustering, very low signal-to-noise ratios, and reflexive feedback between market participants and asset prices. Over roughly six decades, the dominant methodology has moved through five recognizable phases: classical linear econometrics (ARMA, ARIMA, regularized VAR, VECM), conditional volatility modeling (ARCH/GARCH families, Stochastic Volatility), recursive online signal processing (LMS, RLS, Kalman filters), deep sequence learning (LSTMs, TCNs, patch-based Transformers, State Space Models), and the contemporary period (2024–2026) of Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs), Temporal Language Models (TLMs), and LLMs adapted for financial reasoning. For the comparative analysis in Section 10, the deep learning phase is split into two paradigms (recurrent/convolutional networks and Transformer-based architectures), and the foundation model phase into numerical TSFMs and multimodal LLM adapters, yielding seven paradigm entries in total. This paper traces that trajectory through the lens of what we call the Capacity-Adaptability Trilemma, a three-way tension between representational capacity, online adaptability, and structural interpretability. We also review evidence on where foundation models fall short in financial contexts, including benchmark contamination and architectural mismatches that can cause large zero-shot models to underperform simple statistical baselines. To address this, we propose Econometrically-Informed Neural Networks (EINNs) as a way to embed econometric constraints into modern deep architectures. We present four self-contained synthetic experiments run on a MacBook Air M1, which offer only limited, illustrative support for these claims. First, the best model class depends on the data regime: a linear AR/ARMA baseline was best on stationary low-SNR data and across all tested SNR levels in our setup, RLS adapted best under parameter drift, and an LSTM was best only on a high-SNR nonlinear process. Second, a noise-dependent crossover exists between DLinear and PatchTST. Third, trained autoregressors and MLPs do not beat naive persistence on synthetic random walks. Fourth, a proposed VECM regularizer keeps forecast spreads stationary in a bivariate cointegrated setup, though it does so by producing spread forecasts with much lower variance than the true spread. All experiments use synthetic data, and validation on real financial series remains future work.

candidates.title: 效应器自由度与认知扩展循环因果假说(Effector Freedom & Runaway Cognition Loop)(编号107)
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.abstract: Comparative cognition has long treated brain size or neuron number as the primary proxy for cognitive capacity, yet this framework struggles with two persistent anomalies: species with highly flexible effectors that do not develop primate-like cognition (e.g., cats, kangaroos), and species lacking flexible limbs that nonetheless exhibit considerable cognitive complexity (e.g., bottlenose dolphins). We propose the effector–nervous system runaway loop hypothesis: a high-controllability, multifunctional effector or output channel first poses a control problem—compressing a high-dimensional movement space into usable behaviour. Neural expansion is a response to this compression problem; expanded control then re-parameterizes the effector for novel, non-instinctive uses, which generate new environmental feedback and new control demands, driving the loop further. The loop is not self-sustaining: ecological pressure, social-learning demand, lifespan, and energy budget function as stall conditions. We formalize "controllable degrees of freedom" through two hard indices—terminal precision and task-dependent recombination—and evaluate the loop against elephant trunks, primate hands, corvid beaks, and the dolphin acoustic channel. We specify how the hypothesis can be tested against existing datasets (EVApeCognition; Bayesian phylogenetic path analysis) and generate distinguishable predictions from the social brain and cultural drive hypotheses.

candidates.title: แนวทางการรบมอและการปองกนการกลนแกลงในเดก และเยาวชนวยเรยนในจงหวดชลบร
candidates.abstract: This research article aimed to examine coping strategies and prevention approaches for bullying among school-aged children and youth in Chonburi Province, Thailand, and to propose guidelines for developing mechanisms to address and prevent bullying. The study employed a mixed-methods research design conducted in two phases. The first phase was quantitative research, in which data were collected through questionnaires from 907 school-aged children and youth in Chonburi Province and analyzed using descriptive statistics. The second phase was qualitative research, involving in-depth interviews with 30 participants and focus group discussions with 40 participants, including children and youth, parents, teachers, psychologists, social workers, social development practitioners, and representatives from relevant agencies. The qualitative data were analyzed using content analysis. The findings revealed that the most common forms of bullying experienced by children and youth were being ridiculed, mocked, teased about personal weaknesses, or teased about their parents’ names. These were followed by verbal insults and derogatory remarks, as well as threats or gossip. In terms of coping strategies, most children and youth tended to seek alternative ways to avoid risky situations or stay close to trusted friends. This was followed by seeking help from others, communicating with the perpetrator to stop the behavior, and trying to ignore the situation. However, institutional mechanisms, such as reporting channels, homeroom teachers or advisors, and peer support systems, still faced limitations in terms of trust, continuity, and confidentiality. As a result, some children chose to handle the problem on their own or avoided seeking help. The key recommendation of this study is to develop a child-centered system for addressing and preventing bullying by integrating the roles of families, schools, communities, child protection agencies, and relevant professionals. Such a system should include prevention, monitoring, assistance and referral, as well as protection and rehabilitation processes in order to create a safe and child-friendly environment and reduce bullying among school-aged children and youth.

candidates.title: Baby-schema-related cues shape moral expectations about decision-makers: evidence from names, faces, and AI avatars
candidates.abstract: People routinely form expectations about how others will behave in morally difficult situations, and such expectations guide consequential decisions, including whom to trust, hire, or delegate responsibility to. The present research examined whether baby-schema-related cues systematically bias these moral predictions. Across three experiments with Chinese university students (total N = 858), we tested three manifestations of baby-schema-related cues that share the function of evoking infant-like associations: repeated two-syllable names (Experiment 1), babyfaced appearance (Experiment 2), and visually cute artificial intelligence (AI) avatar designs (Experiment 3). Participants consistently perceived decision-makers displaying baby-schema-related cues as less likely to make utilitarian choices involving direct harm to others. The results show that superficially irrelevant social cues can bias moral expectations about others, although the underlying psychological mechanism remains to be clarified. These findings are relevant to moral psychology, person perception, and the design and evaluation of AI systems.

candidates.title: Bacteria inside kidney tumors associate with myeloid inflammation and disease progression: A TRACERx Renal study
candidates.abstract: BackgroundIntratumoral bacteria are increasingly recognized as active contributors to neutrophil-driven inflammation and disease progression in solid tumors. Yet, in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), where myeloid inflammation is a key feature of aggressive disease, live bacterial presence, their intratumoral distribution, and interaction with the tumor microenvironment remain unexplored.MethodsWe genetically characterized the microbiome of primary ccRCC tumors across two independent cohorts (TRACERx: 616 samples, 143 patients; The Cancer Genome Atlas [TCGA]: 511 samples and patients), confirming live bacterial presence through culture. Multi-regional sampling enabled within-tumor analysis of bacterial distribution. Associations with the tumor microenvironment were explored at scale using bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) across both cohorts and corroborated in depth through spatial transcriptomics and in vitro infection assays.FindingsAcross both cohorts, the commensal Cutibacterium emerged as the dominant genus, accumulating in discrete niches enriched toward the tumor center and associating with more advanced (TRACERx p = 0.024; TCGA p = 0.0011) tumors and shorter progression-free survival (TRACERx p = 0.0022; TCGA p = 4.4 × 10-4). Both across and within tumors, Cutibacterium accumulation associated with neutrophil recruitment and myeloid inflammation. In vitro, Cutibacterium induced sustained expression of neutrophil-attracting chemokines in macrophages, recapitulating patient tumor findings.ConclusionsThese findings establish intratumoral bacteria as novel prognostic components of the ccRCC tumor microenvironment and suggest an active role in shaping local myeloid inflammation, laying the groundwork for investigating their potential as therapeutic targets.FundingThis work was supported by the Francis Crick Institute (Cancer Research UK, MRC, Wellcome Trust). TRACERx Renal is funded by Cancer Research UK (C50947/A18176).

candidates.title: Patching With Sequential Updating for High-Fidelity Bayesian Spectral Estimation of Physiological Time Series
candidates.abstract: Physiological time series reflect the underlying behavior of physiological systems. In this paper, we introduce a novel patching with sequential updating for Bayesian nonparametric spectral estimation (PBNSE) to enhance spectral estimation and interpretation of imperfect physiological time series with fragmented, noncontiguous segments. PBNSE incorporates four key strategies: (1) modeling patches as patch-specific Gaussian processes (GPs); (2) patch-dependence, where each patch involves a joint GP with a shared kernel, capturing both observation and spectral dependencies across all patches; (3) sequential parameter shift that transfers knowledge between patches while maintaining computational traceability; and (4) aggregating patch-level posterior spectra into a unified power spectral density (PSD) estimate and computing the expectation of the PSD in a closed form. Extensive experiments demonstrate significant improvements in spectral accuracy and robustness compared to state-of-the-art methods such as BNSE, multitaper, periodogram, Lomb-Scargle, functional kernel learning (FKL), and variational sparse spectrum (SVSS). PBNSE addresses key challenges in physiological signal analysis, including irregular sampling, incomplete signal, and varying noise. The widespread adoption of PBNSE in physiological signal research has the potential to enhance the accuracy of spectral estimation and improve the robustness of interpreting complex, real-world physiological time series.

candidates.title: Restoring One Health: The Impact of Food Safety Legislation on Bison as an Indigenous Food Source in Western Canada
candidates.abstract: Abstract    The  Food Policy for Canada  intends to support the revitalization of Indigenous food systems and address food insecurity. From a food safety perspective, multiple barriers exist that prevent Indigenous Peoples from exercising traditional hunting, harvesting, and slaughtering practices for traditional animal-derived foods. The current provincial (British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba) and federal (Canada) food safety regulatory environment poses restrictions on the raising, slaughtering, and processing of livestock, of which bison may be classified, that hinder the ability of First Nations and the Métis Nation to define their food systems. Licenses and restrictions, land accessibility and infrastructural costs hinder Indigenous Peoples from exercising food sovereignty and participating in the broader food system. Reducing barriers, while leveraging a minority of current regulations (e.g. on-farm slaughter in British Columbia and bison classified as a livestock product), are first steps to enabling food sovereignty, economic growth, and allowing communities to achieve wholistic One Health outcomes related to nutrition, identity, and health of the natural environment. Thus, universally benefitting rural and isolated populations irrespective of cultural background. Capacity-building founded on a sense of trust and common knowledge related to acceptable level of risk could allow Indigenous communities to identify hazards associated with traditional foods and make decisions on how to best control them within their food system.  Clinical trial number:  not applicable.

candidates.title: Real Computation or Merely Naming? A Pre-Registered Mechanism Audit of 25 Cognitive-Architecture Modules in an LLM-Based Agent System
candidates.abstract: Agent systems built on local large language models are increasingly marketed through the vocabulary of cognitive architecture: modules named global workspace, theory of mind, causal reasoning, or active inference are listed as features, and the presence of the name is taken as the presence of the mechanism. We ask the prior question -- does the named computation actually happen -- and contribute a transferable verification method for the claim-implementation gap: a four-question static audit protocol with line-number evidence and call-chain tracing, demonstrated on two systems. We audit a system claiming 25 cognitive mechanisms, pre-register falsifiable predictions for 11 modules and execute the interventions, replicate the protocol on the IIT-phi core of a second, independent system with its own pre-committed falsification criteria, and run two repair experiments as positive controls. In 18 of 25 modules the computed value never reaches any production output; three idle-wiring shapes new to the dead-code and code-smell literatures emerge (connected-but-never-called, called-but-inert, called-but-content-blind). Of 61 frozen criteria across 12 interventions, 53 were confirmed, two partially adjudicated, five falsified, one adjudication-ambiguous. Repairs raised planner task success from 0.028 to 1.000 and cut state-controller error by 52%. Module names and module computations must be audited as independent claims; the protocol and the five-class failure taxonomy are reusable for the claim-implementation gap at two-system, case-level depth.

candidates.title: PromptSense: Sentiment-Aware Mental Health Chatbot with Dynamic Prompting
candidates.abstract: Current Large Language Models (LLMs)-based mental health chatbots often lack sufficient empathy, contextual awareness, and safety mechanisms, potentially leading to ineffective or harmful interactions. This paper proposes a novel framework that integrates sentiment and depression analysis with a rule-based filtering mechanism prior to model inference. By dynamically constructing prompts based on emotional and risk-related insights, the framework aims to significantly improve the contextual relevance, empathy, and risk-aware of model-generated responses. We evaluated four model strategies and two prompt engineered variants across qualitative metrics such as empathy, helpfulness, clarity, relevance, safety, as well as toxicity assessments using the Perspective API. Experimental results indicate that the prompt engineering approaches outperforms DSFT and RLAIF by 1.8\% and 1.1\% respectively.
